ABSTRACT
Ultra-­high molecular weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) has long been used as a bearing component in joint replacement devices, 
particularly in total hip arthroplasty (THA) and total knee arthroplasty (TKA). These implants are conventionally manufactured 
using the machining route, and an alternative approaches to produce net-­shaped UHMWPE implants has been explored to a 
limited extent. In this context, its high melt viscosity poses significant challenges in molding complex and thicker components, 
with uncompromised mechanical strength and ductility. To address both these aspects, a new processing strategy has been pre-
sented here, where a tailored amount of short-­chain polyethylene grafted maleic anhydride (mPE) is introduced into UHMWPE 
via the melt compounding technique to enhance moldability. We optimized the injection molding parameters—including melt 
temperature, mold temperature, injection pressure, and injection time—within a narrow window to achieve a UHMWPE blend 
with enhanced mechanical properties. When compared to pristine UHMWPE 4% mPE blend exhibited a better melt flow index 
from 6.2 to 8.2 g/10 min and enhanced ultimate tensile strength (27.5 to 31.4 MPa) and elongation at break (46.4% to 77.7%). 
Additionally, the crystallinity of the mPE blends decreased to 51%, facilitating better flow characteristics, as indicated by a reduc-
tion in complex viscosity from 18.83 to 12.30 kPa·s. Using the optimised molding parameters, we successfully molded acetabular 
liners of commercial design with acceptable dimensional tolerances (shrinkage: 2.1%–2.4%; ovality: 0.06–0.09 mm) and without 
detectable internal defects, as analysed using micro-­computed tomography (micro-­CT). The present work highlights the poten-
tial of mPE blends in injection molding for producing high-­performance orthopedic implants, addressing a critical gap in scalable 
manufacturing processes for components of varying sizes and shapes in biomedical applications.
1   |   Introduction
The significant rise in the aging global population needs de-
mand for joint replacement surgeries, and such demands are 
driven by demography and the prevalence of physical trauma, 
including injuries, accidents, and conditions such as obesity 
and osteoarthritis [1–6]. By 2030, it is projected that the need 
for primary total hip joint replacements (THR) will rise by 171% 
among individuals under 65 years of age [7–9]. THR is widely 
recognized as one of the most effective surgical interventions for 
load-­bearing orthopedic applications [5, 10, 11]. The main goals 
of orthopedic implants are to offer mechanical support that

A variety of materials, including composite [5, 13–15], ceramic

applications depending on their mechanical properties, physi-
cochemical characteristics, biodegradability, reactivity, and vis-
coelastic behavior, which mimic natural human tissues such as 
bone, cartilage, and ligaments [5, 6, 17, 19, 20]. Materials with 
high wear resistance and tensile properties are essential for 
articulating joints [21, 22]. Polymeric materials have gained 
widespread acceptance in biomedical applications due to their 
versatility, viz. easy machinability, biocompatibility, etc., and 
they are commonly used in artificial joints, acetabular compo-
nents, and tissue scaffolds [5, 23, 24].
In this context, UHMWPE has been clinically used as an ace-
tabular liner in THR for over 60 years, owing to its advantageous 
mechanochemical and tribological properties, high impact re-
sistance, and biocompatibility [5, 25]. Due to these exceptional 
combinations of properties of UHMWPE, components are pri-
marily used for orthopedic applications such as hip and knee 
joint replacement [5, 16]. Despite its widespread application in 
various joint arthroplasties, including total knee joint arthro-
plasty (TKR) [5], total shoulder arthroplasty (TSK) [4], and total 
hip replacement(THR) [5, 16], the performance of UHMWPE 
is often compromised by significant challenges. These include 
issues related to wear resistance [26, 27] and adverse cellular 
responses [12, 28] to wear debris generated during articulation.
The selection of materials for acetabular liners in total hip ar-
throplasty (THA) is critical for implant longevity and reliable 
clinical performance. For example, UHMWPE has been the 
standard due to its excellent wear resistance and biocompatibil-
ity, and the last few decades have witnessed more advancements 
like highly cross-­linked polyethylene (HXLPE) [5, 25, 29] in an 
effort to reduce wear rates [25, 30]. Additionally, ceramic mate-
rials such as alumina and zirconia are increasingly used to min-
imize wear, and ceramic-­on-­ceramic configurations are being 
developed but not widely used clinically. Alternative polymers 
like polyurethane (PUR) [31, 32] and polyether-­ether-­ketone 
(PEEK) [23, 33] are also being explored for their potential ben-
efits. Many companies have commercial-­scale manufacturing 
facility options [23, 24, 34]. THA includes Stryker, Exactech, 
Smith & Nephew, Zimmer Biomet, and Lima Corporate, featur-
ing various polyethylene and ceramic liners.
Currently, the commercial method for producing UHMWPE 
implants involves machining UHMWPE rods into specific 
shapes and sizes [5, 23]. However, this traditional manufactur-
ing approach is associated with significant material loss and 
degradation of mechanical properties, raising concerns about 
its cost-­effectiveness [5, 15, 35]. Furthermore, the challenges re-
lated to wear resistance and oxidative degradation of UHMWPE 
must be addressed to enhance its performance in biomedical 
applications [14, 25, 36, 37]. Due to its high molecular weight, 
UHMWPE exhibits considerable viscosity, which complicates 
processing via conventional screw extrusion or injection mold-
ing techniques [5, 15].
Given these challenges, there is an urgent need for innovative 
manufacturing techniques that can enhance the processability 
of UHMWPE while minimizing material waste and preserv-
ing its mechanical integrity. Injection molding has emerged as 
a promising alternative manufacturing method, offering rapid 
and efficient production of near-­net shapes without requiring 
extensive post-­processing [38, 39]. However, the intrinsic prop-
erties of UHMWPE, characterized by its high molecular weight 
and viscosity, have historically posed significant obstacles to its 
suitability for injection molding applications [40, 41]. This poor 
processability limits the potential for extensive hybridization of 
UHMWPE with other materials, thereby constraining its appli-
cation in orthopedic implants.
Recent advancements in processing techniques have made it 
possible to covalently graft polyethylene chains onto graphene 
oxide (GO) nanosheets, significantly enhancing material prop-
erties. An optimized blend containing 40% UHMWPE and 
60 wt% blended with 1 wt% of modified GO has remarkably im-
proved mechanical performance. Specifically, the incorporation 
of modified GO elevated the tensile strength to approximately 
60 MPa; however, this enhancement was accompanied by a re-
duced elongation to less than 100%. Furthermore, these com-
posites' observed favorable cell attachment underscores their 
potential applicability in geoengineering [22, 35]. One notice-
able challenge with this composite is the black color of the blend 
due to the incorporation of GO, which, though clinically viable, 
was commercially unacceptable.
Contemporary advancements in ultra-­high-­molecular-­weight 
polyethylene (UHMWPE) have focused on improving its 
performance for orthopedic implants. Hybrid over-­molding 
with 3D-­printed polyetheretherketone (PEEK) has enhanced 
interfacial bonding and mechanical properties, offering an 
alternative to traditional metal-­backed components (Smith 
et al.) [33]. The incorporation of self-­lubricating materials like 
cubic titanium carbide (c-­TiC) and multiwalled carbon nano-
tubes (MWCNTs) has reduced material loss by 41.7%, improv-

composites reinforced with talc, graphite, and MWCNTs have 
shown a 30% reduction in friction and a 54% decrease in wear, 
highlighting their potential for enhancing acetabular liner 
performance (Nayak et al.) [44]. Integrating inorganic fillers 
has also been explored to improve UHMWPE composites' me-

2   |   Materials and Methods
2.1   |   Materials
GUR 1050 (Medical grade UHMWPE, average molecular 
weight (Mw)): 5 × 106 g/mol was procured from Celanese Ticona 
Polymers, USA. Maleated polyethylene (mPE), specifically 
OPTIM E-­119, was obtained from Pluss Polymers in India. This 
mPE has a melt flow index (MFI) of 2 g/10 min (~Mw: 3–5 × 104 g/
mol), medium mPE content, and a 0.932 g/cm3 density. All other 
reagents and analytical-­grade chemicals were utilized in their 
received state without additional purification steps.
2.2   |   Injection Molding of UHMWPE
Medical-­grade GUR 1050 or pristine UHMWPE pellets were 
processed using an Xplore microinjection molding machine, op-
erating at an injection pressure ranging from 12 to 14 bar. The 
melt temperature varied between 220°C and 280°C, while the 
molding temperature was adjusted from room temperature (RT) 
to 80°C to produce dumbbell-­shaped specimens as per ASTM 
D638-­03 standards. It was assumed that the material behaves 
as a non-­Newtonian fluid with high viscosity for the injection 
molding of pristine UHMWPE. During injection into the mold 
cavity, it was assumed that there is instantaneous cavity filling, 
isotropic cooling of the part, and an ambient temperature of 
27°C to simplify the calculation. Additionally, various combina-
tions of injection pressure, holding time, melt temperature, and 
mold temperature were employed to optimize the tensile proper-
ties of pristine UHMWPE, including elastic modulus, UTS, and 
elongation at failure.
2.3   |   Preparation of mPE Blends and Injection 
Molding
The blends of mPE and pristine UHMWPE were formulated 
using established melt-­mixing methods. Specifically, mPE was 
combined with UHMWPE at various weight percentages (0%, 
1%, 2%, 4%, and 5%) at a processing temperature of 260°C for 
10 min of mixing time. Throughout the melt-­mixing process, a 
constant force of approximately 6 kN and a screw rotation speed 
of 60 rpm were maintained to ensure thorough blending. The 
resulting mixtures were then compression-­molded under the 
same temperature and pressure conditions as injection molding, 
assuming there were no significant processing effects on the 
rheological properties of these samples for a holding time of 10 
to 15 min under an applied pressure of 40 to 50 bar to produce 
disc specimens with a diameter of 15–25 mm and a thickness 
of 1 mm.
2.4   |   Mechanical Testing
Uniaxial tensile testing was conducted with a 5 kN load cell 
using an INSTRON model 5967 machine. Dumbbell-­shaped 
specimens created through microinjection molding were tested 
at a 50 mm/min crosshead speed until fracture, following the 
ASTM D638 guidelines. Additionally, the fracture surfaces of 
the molded samples were examined using a scanning electron 
microscope (SEM) operating in secondary electron mode at an 
accelerating voltage of 5 kV.
2.5   |   Rheological Properties
Rheological properties were analyzed using a TA Instruments 
HR-­3 DISCOVERY hybrid rheometer with a 25 mm diameter 
parallel plate and an Instron SR20 single-­bore capillary rheom-
eter with a length-­to-­diameter (L/D) ratio of 10:1. The parallel 
plate rheometer measured viscoelastic properties at lower shear 
rates (0–1000 s−1), while the capillary rheometer assessed vis-
cosity at higher shear rates (1000 to 10,000 s−1). The selection 
of these two rheometers is critical, as the capillary rheometer is 
particularly well suited for emulating the extreme conditions en-
countered during injection molding, which are characterized by 
elevated shear rates and pressures. These instruments measure 
complex viscosity, which combines two key parameters: the stor-
age modulus (G′), which represents how much energy the mate-
rial can store when deformed, and the loss modulus (G″), which 
shows how much power is lost as heat during deformation.
The viscoelastic properties, including shear thinning behavior 
and the temperature and frequency-­dependent variations of 
loss modulus (G″), storage modulus (G′), and complex viscos-
ity of the pristine UHMWPE and mPE blends were analyzed 
using Parallel plate rheometer. For the viscoelastic evaluations,

The MFI of the UHMWPE and the mPE blend was evaluated by

For the MFI analysis, 3–5 g of each polymer sample was accu-
rately weighed and placed into the barrel of a Melt Flow Index

mPE blend to ensure the polymers reached their melting points. 
After a preheating period of 5 min, a standard weight of 21.6 kg 
was applied to a piston positioned above the molten polymer. This 
weight exerted pressure on the sample, forcing it through a die 
with a standardized opening diameter of approximately 2 mm. 
The MFI tester automatically calculates the MFI value at various 
intervals and obtains the average MFI value for the polymer.

2.12   |   Quality Assessment Injection Molded 
Acetabular Liner
2.12.1   |   Dimensional Tolerance
To assess the dimensional tolerance and shrinkage of the 
injection-­molded acetabular liner, various quality control in-
struments were employed, including a Coordinate Measuring 
Machine (CMM), Vernier Caliper (VC), Micro-­Probe (MP), and 
Video Measuring System (VMS). These instruments were uti-
lized to evaluate critical dimensions such as inner diameter (ID), 
outer diameter (OD), spherical surface dimensions, and groove 
sizes, which are essential for calculating shrinkage and ovality 
in the molded part.
2.12.2   |   Shrinkage Analysis
Shrinkage analysis of the molded acetabular liner was per-
formed to assess dimensional stability following the injection 
molding process. After allowing the molded parts to cool to 
room temperature, the ID and OD were measured using cal-
ibrated digital calipers. The actual physical mold dimensions 
are considered initial dimensions, and the final dimensions 
are the actual injection molded part dimensions measured 
using the various quality control instruments (VC, CMM, 
VMS, MP), as mentioned in Section 2.12.1 Dimensional tol-
erances of ±0.2 mm for ID and OD were established based 
on industry standards for orthopedic implants. Ovality was 
assessed by comparing ID measurements from both the in-
jection gate and non-­gate sides to ensure proper fit within or-
thopedic applications. The percentage shrinkage for various 
critical dimensions of the molded liner was calculated using 
Equation (4).
2.12.3   |   Dimensional Compatibility Analysis
The compatibility of the molded acetabular liner with acetabu-
lar assembly components was assessed manually using metal-
lic and ceramic femoral heads, each with an outer diameter of 
32 mm. The evaluation involved inserting the femoral heads into 
the acetabular liner and observing their movement and fit by 
rotating and moving the heads within the liner. Key observa-
tions included the smoothness of motion and the force required 
for movement. Quantitative measurements were taken to deter-
mine the difference between the outer diameter of the femoral 
heads and the inner diameter of the molded acetabular liner. 
These qualitative assessments and quantitative measurements 
comprehensively evaluated dimensional compatibility between 
the molded acetabular liner and the femoral heads, ensuring 
suitability for orthopedic applications.
2.12.4   |   Micro-­Computed Tomography (3D 
Microstructure) Analysis
The three-­dimensional structural analysis of the injection-­
molded acetabular liner prototype, utilizing the optimized 4% 
mPE blend and UHHMWPE pellets, was conducted via 3D vol-
ume rendering using X-­ray micro-­computed tomography (μCT) 
(VersaXRM-­500, Xradia, Zeiss, Germany). Image acquisition 
for the acetabular liners was performed over approximately 3 h, 
with a step size of 0.11°, resulting from 3201 projections. The 
scanning was executed with an X-­ray source operating at 80 kV 
and 7 W power. A combination of a 0.39X objective with an ex-
posure time of 1 s was utilized to achieve a voxel size of 46.4 μm. 
The resulting 3D tomogram was reconstructed from the trans-
mission orthoslices using commercially available software 
‘XMReconstructor’ (Xradia, Zeiss). The software employed 
a filtered back-­projection algorithm with a kernel size of 0.5, 
alongside standard beam hardening correction and Gaussian 
smoothing for enhanced reconstruction quality.
3   |   Results and Discussion
Recent research initiatives have focused on addressing the 
challenges associated with UHMWPE by exploring various 
strategies to enhance its flowability and mechanical proper-
ties through blending with other polymers [13, 23, 41, 53]. For 
example, a few studies have demonstrated that incorporating 
low molecular weight polyethylene or reinforcing UHMWPE 
with carbon nanotubes (CNTs) [13, 23, 41, 53]. Despite these 
advancements, commercially available orthopedic prod-
ucts utilizing injection-­molded UHMWPE still need to be 
expanded, highlighting the need for further innovation in 
this area.
Extensive investigations into UHMWPE blends with other poly-
olefin families, such as linear low-­density polyethylene (LLDPE) 
[54] and high-­density polyethylene (HDPE) [15, 22, 35, 54], have 
emphasized their mechanical characteristics. For instance, one 
study [46] Reported that with an increase in the UHMWPE con-
tent within the LDPE matrix, the elongation reduced from 700% 
to 200%, while the tensile strength marginally increased from 
12 MPa to 15 MPa. These findings indicate that while blend-
ing can improve specific mechanical properties, it often comes 
at the expense of ductility. Therefore, achieving a balance be-
tween processability and performance remains a critical chal-
lenge in developing UHMWPE-­based composites for orthopedic 
applications.
The density measurement using Archimedes principle showed 
that the density decreased from 0.95 to 0.93 g/cm3 as the mPE 
content increased from 0% to 5%. This minor reduction can 
be attributed to the incorporation of mPE, which introduces a 
lower-­density component into the blend, slightly altering the 
overall density without significantly affecting the material's 
structural integrity.
The MFI, which is a crucial parameter for evaluating the pro-
cessability of polymer blends for injection molding, ranged from 
7.6 to 8.2 g/10 min at 190°C under a 21.6 kg load for mPE blended 
UHMWPE, as compared to 6.2 g/10 min for pristine UHMWPE.

3.1   |   Injection Molding of UHMWPE: 
Optimization of Injection Molding Parameters
The two-­fold objectives, namely enhancing processability and 
optimizing mechanical properties of UHMWPE during in-
jection molding, require a precise optimization of injection 
molding parameters. For the initial aim of making UHMWPE 
injection moldable, the mold (RT-­80°C) and melt temperatures 
(220°C–280°C), including cooling, holding times, and total in-
jection pressure, were strategically adjusted. This resulted in 
optimized mechanical properties of the molded component, 
namely elastic modulus, tensile strength, and elongation.

3.3.6   |   Characteristic Shear-­Thinning 
Behavior Analysis
In the parallel plate tests, both mPE blends and pristine 
UHMWPE demonstrated a typical shear-­thinning behav-
ior characterized by a reduction in viscosity as the shear rate 
increased (see Figure  7a,b). This behavior is typical for poly-
meric materials and can be related to the alignment of polymer 
chains in the direction of flow [50, 65]. At lower shear rates, the 
polymer chains are entangled and oriented randomly, resulting 
in higher viscosity due to increased resistance to flow. However, 
as the shear rate increases, these chains begin to align and dis-
entangle, leading to reduced intermolecular friction and lower 
viscosity.
The results from the capillary rheometer further corroborated 
this trend. It was observed that pristine UHMWPE did not 
flow until the shear rate exceeded 1000 s−1, with flow initia-
tion occurring at 2000 s−1 (see Figure 7b). In contrast, the 4% 
mPE blend melted at a shear rate of 1000 s−1. This significant 
difference in flow behavior can be explained by several inter-
related factors: Pristine UHMWPE possesses a higher molec-
ular weight and a greater chain entanglement compared to the

3.3.7   |   Temperature-­Dependent Viscoelastic Behavior
The results from the temperature sweep analysis indicated 
that as the temperature increased, the viscosity of both the 
mPE blends and pristine UHMWPE decreased (see Figure 8a). 
This behavior is characteristic of polymers, where higher tem-
peratures facilitate molecular motion, reducing intermolecu-
lar interactions and friction among polymer chains [65, 66]. As 
thermal energy increases, the polymer chains gain mobility, 
allowing them to easily slide past each other. This reduces vis-
cosity, which is essential for processing applications such as 
injection molding, where lower viscosity at elevated tempera-
tures can enhance flow characteristics and fill complex mold 
geometries more effectively. Moreover, the analysis revealed 
that viscosity also decreased with increasing mPE content in 
the blends. This reduction can be attributed to shorter mo-
lecular chains in the mPE blend than in pristine UHMWPE. 
Shorter chains tend to have lower entanglement density and 
reduced cohesive forces, enhancing flow properties. As more 
mPE is incorporated into the blend, its plasticizing effect 
becomes more pronounced, further lowering viscosity and 
improving processability [50, 65, 66]. The combination of in-
creased temperature and higher mPE content results in a syn-
ergistic effect that optimizes the flow behavior of the polymer 
matrix.
During temperature sweep analysis (220°C–280°C), both G' 
and G” exhibited a decreasing trend with increasing tempera-
ture. This decrease in moduli can be explained by enhanced 
molecular mobility at elevated temperatures. With increased 
temperature, polymer chains acquire kinetic energy, enhanc-
ing chain mobility and diminishing intermolecular inter-
actions. Consequently, this results in a softer material that 
exhibits lower resistance to deformation. Despite this de-
crease, G' consistently remained higher than G” throughout 
the entire temperature range. This relationship signifies that 
even as thermal agitation increases and both moduli decrease, 
the material retains its elastic characteristics over viscous

decreased across both frequency and temperature sweeps,

higher moduli values. The plasticizing effect of mPE further

4   |   Conclusions
This work has presented a comprehensive study on the injec-
tion moldability of UHMWPE. Short-­chain polyethylene graft-
ing based UHMWPE blend formulation (mPE) has been used 
to address the inherent challenges associated with the injection 
molding of UHMWPE by effectively reducing melt viscosity. 
The tailored addition of 3%–4% mPE rendered UHMWPE suit-
able for a plunger-­based injection molding, facilitating the re-
producible production of tensile test samples. Importantly, the 
addition of maleated short-­chain polyethylene did not signifi-
cantly alter the molecular structure of molded UHMWPE, as 
confirmed by spectroscopy and thermal analysis. The optimized 
4% mPE blend demonstrated a notable enhancement in mechan-
ical properties, UTS increasing from 27.5 to 31.4 MPa and elon-
gation at break improving from 46.4% to 77.7%. Moreover, the 
MFI for the 4% mPE blend exhibited a significant enhancement, 
indicating improved material processability and flow charac-
teristics. Rheological analyses involving parallel plate and cap-
illary rheometer tests established a critical process window for 
injection molding parameters that can be effectively translated 
to commercial-­scale manufacturing. This approach enabled the 
production of dimensionally compliant, defect-­free acetabular 
liner prototypes in a reproducible manner. The dimensional 
tolerances achieved for external surface features conformed to 
commercial design specifications, reinforcing the viability of 
injection molding as a scalable, high-­throughput manufactur-
ing process capable of producing net-­shaped UHMWPE com-
ponents with thicknesses up to 8 mm. This study underscores 
the recyclability and sustainability of the proposed manufac-
turing route. By utilizing recyclable polyethylene blends, which 
are thermoplastic and can be remelted and repurposed, we can 
significantly minimize waste generated during manufacturing, 
thereby aligning with sustainable manufacturing practices. 
Additionally, the capacity to produce defect-­free components 
with consistent dimensional tolerances enhances the system's 
viability for long-­term applications in high-­throughput produc-
tion environments.
The practical implications of this research are demonstrated 
through the successful production of dimensionally compliant 
acetabular liner prototypes within 2 min, without generating 
waste typically associated with conventional machining pro-
cesses. These prototypes exhibited exceptional dimensional sta-
bility, with shrinkage ranging from 2.1% to 2.4% and minimal 
ovality between 0.06 and 0.09 mm, ensuring compatibility with 
both ceramic and metallic femoral heads. Furthermore, struc-
tural integrity was confirmed using 3D microcomputed tomog-
raphy (micro-­CT), which detected no processing defects such as 
cracks or voids, thereby validating their suitability for clinical 
applications. The insights gained from polymer processing and 
injection molding processes provide a foundation for develop-
ing other complex-­shaped components with varying thicknesses 
from high-­viscosity polymers like UHMWPE in emerging 
healthcare-­related applications.

Abstract: Ultra-­high molecular weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) has long been used as a bearing component in joint replacement devices, particularly in total hip arthroplasty (THA) and total knee arthroplasty (TKA). These implants are conventionally manufactured using the machining route, and an alternative approaches to produce net-­shaped UHMWPE implants has been explored to a limited extent. In this context, its high melt viscosity poses significant challenges in molding complex and thicker components, with uncompromised mechanical strength and ductility. To address both these aspects, a new processing strategy has been pre- sented here, where a tailored amount of short-­chain polyethylene grafted maleic anhydride (mPE) is introduced into UHMWPE via the melt compounding technique to enhance moldability. We optimized the injection molding parameters—including melt temperature, mold temperature, injection pressure, and injection time—within a narrow window to achieve a UHMWPE blend with enhanced mechanical properties. When compared to pristine UHMWPE 4% mPE blend exhibited a better melt flow index from 6.2 to 8.2 g/10 min and enhanced ultimate tensile strength (27.5 to 31.4 MPa) and elongation at break (46.4% to 77.7%). Additionally, the crystallinity of the mPE blends decreased to 51%, facilitating better flow characteristics, as indicated by a reduc- tion in complex viscosity from 18.83 to 12.30 kPa·s. Using the optimised molding parameters, we successfully molded acetabular liners of commercial design with acceptable dimensional tolerances (shrinkage: 2.1%–2.4%; ovality: 0.06–0.09 mm) and without detectable internal defects, as analysed using micro-­computed tomography (micro-­CT). The present work highlights the poten- tial of mPE blends in injection molding for producing high-­performance orthopedic implants, addressing a critical gap in scalable manufacturing processes for components of varying sizes and shapes in biomedical applications.
